title: Three Ways to Lose a Romance Reader
rule: Romance must end with the couple together and committed (HEA or HFN): no separating them at the end, no killing a love interest, no leaving readers unsure the relationship survives. The reader's heart is never divided (no rival intimate involvement unless the structure is announced up front). The couple shares scenes; chapters apart drain the chemistry, so count shared scenes in revision.
example: A story that ends with the relationship's survival in doubt is a fine novel but not a romance ending.

title: Advice from the Archives: HEA vs. HFN (Harlequin)
rule: A Harlequin editor says the choice between HEA and HFN depends on the story; a promise of a new, better beginning can satisfy more than a ring and forever. Page returned 403, so this is the search summary only; it is the one acquiring-editor source found. No publisher guideline found that explicitly bans killing the hero; RWA's definition is a central love story with an 'emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending'.

title: If It Doesn't Have an HEA (or HFN), It's Not Romance
rule: A majority of readers read romance for the HEA and trust the author to deliver it; breaking that trust angers readers. No reader survey data was found.

title: Father Knox's Decalogue
rule: Knox (1928/29): the culprit is named early but is not a viewpoint character; no supernatural agencies; at most one secret passage; no undiscovered poisons or long scientific explanations; no accident or unaccountable intuition helps the detective; the detective is not the culprit; no clue found that the reader is not shown at once; the Watson hides no thoughts; doubles only if prepared. Often read as partly tongue-in-cheek and broken by Christie; dates differ by source, and rule 5 is racist and dropped.
example: Svoresky's The Sins of Father Knox breaks one rule per story as a game.

title: A Magician's Contract Between Reader and Writer: Rules for Delivering a Whodunit
rule: Van Dine and Knox reduce to 'there must be fair play': every clue the detective uses is shown to the reader; a motive, however flimsy; the culprit is an identified suspect, not a bystander who vanishes ('the delivery boy'). Red herrings, lying suspects and a detective who withholds his theory are allowed. Readers punish cheating (Ackroyd split readers) and motiveless killers, and also an answer solvable in thirty pages.
example: Hidden is fine, absent is cheating: clues may be concealed, misdirected or delayed, but must be on the page.

title: Modeling Fair Play in Detective Stories (Wagner, Keydar, Abend)
rule: Probabilistic fair-play score (how much the clues shift a reader toward the culprit) applied to LLM detective stories. Read only the first 100k of 116k characters.
example: GPT-4o often settles on the culprit during the introduction; Llama stories reuse one detective name (Jameson in about 90%).
llm_tell: LLM detective stories fail to balance surprise and fair play: misleading is easy, but clues that limit the outcome are weak; later paragraphs add little; the culprit converges for reasons other than the clues; endings are over-creative and contradict the clues.

title: The Cozy Mystery Explained (PBS Masterpiece) with Wikipedia, Reedsy, TV Tropes
rule: Descriptive, not a rulebook: sex and violence offstage, the murder itself undescribed (only the body found), little or no swearing, an amateur sleuth often with a hobby or small business, a small intimate community where everyone knows everyone, an unpleasant victim, peril kept mild, the amateur solves it before the police and order is restored. Wikipedia: boundaries of the subgenre are vague.

title: Kishotenketsu: The Structure That Grabs Attention Without Conflict
rule: Ki introduces the world without disrupting it; sho deepens rather than escalates ('rhythm, not revolution', no sudden twists); ten reframes what came before rather than just moving the plot; ketsu reconciles the threads without being forced. Interest comes from 'how do these connect?', not opposition. Failures: rushing sho, a ten that only advances plot, a contrived ketsu.
example: Spirited Away: No-Face and Haku's hidden identity at ten; Chihiro finds harmony, not victory. Doraemon 'Anywhere Door': the twist is a circumstance, not a villain. Other sources note it is a driving-conflict absence, not an absence of all friction, and it traces to Chinese qi-cheng-zhuan-he poetry.
llm_tell: Not tested anywhere I found. Inference only (unverified): a model's conflict-escalation default, and its measured tidy upbeat resolution, would turn a ten into a villain and a ketsu into a moral.

title: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction
rule: 10,272 prompts, each answered by a human and five LLMs. Discourse features (character agency, chronological structure) separate human from AI at 93.2% macro-F1 without style; narrative features alone keep over 97% of the full model's attribution performance. Abstract only; no genre breakdown reported.
llm_tell: AI stories over-explain themes, favour neat single-storyline plots, have simpler social structures and less moral ambiguity; humans show more temporal complexity. Per model: Claude notably flat event escalation, GPT dream sequences, Gemini external character description.

title: Creative Convergence or Imitation? Genre-Specific Homogeneity in LLM-Generated Chinese Literature
rule: Extends Propp to 34 narrative functions for modern web fiction. Abstract does not say which genres were compared or ranked; the genre split lives in the full paper, not read.
llm_tell: LLM stories repeat the same arrangements of plot events and end in stereotypical resolutions, attributed to the model not grasping what each narrative function means and following rigid generation patterns.

title: Art or Artifice? (Chakrabarty et al., CHI'24)
rule: Expert annotators separated AI from human stories by creative execution rather than surface cues; no genre breakdown found in the abstract or summaries I read.
llm_tell: Recurring expert complaints: weak endings, clichéd or incoherent metaphors, thin characters without subtext.

title: Thriller pacing sources (careerauthors, Baldacci MasterClass, others)
rule: Ticking clock as the core device; shorten the timetable just as the characters seem close; short scenes and quick dialogue; end a scene on a question and let each answer open another; the villain can be on a clock too. Craft-blog level, no measured source. Failure named: 'hurry up and wait', a countdown set up and then stalled.
example: Timestamp chapter headings such as '18 hours until detonation'.

title: Why novels get rejected / editor slush-pile accounts (several, search results)
rule: Most-cited cause in summaries of first-novel rejections: exposition and backstory crowding the first dozen pages; also overwritten openings, unclear viewpoint, unconvincing motive, unresolved loose ends. Agents say five to ten pages is enough to decide. Individual editors and agents, not a study; no literary-fiction-specific editor source found.
